I always salute these sages, Krishna, makers of the world, eldest of the world, devoted to knowledge, dispellers of darkness, suns of the world.
mahabharata:13:32.25	Therefore you too, Varshneya, always honour the twice-born; honoured, they who are worthy of honour will give you happiness, sinless one.
mahabharata:13:32.26	In this world they always, and in the next, give happiness; when honoured they will give happiness to you.
mahabharata:13:32.27	Those who are hosts of all, always devoted to cows and brahmanas and to truth, cross over hard places.
mahabharata:13:32.28	Those who are always intent on peace and those without envy, and those who always study, cross over hard places.
mahabharata:13:32.29	Those who bow to all the gods and those who resort to one god, faithful and self-controlled, cross over hard places.
mahabharata:13:32.30	So too those who, saluting the best brahmins of controlled vows, are devoted to giving, cross over hard places.
mahabharata:13:32.31	Those who, having duly established the fires, keep them purely, and have attained the Soma offering, cross over hard places.
mahabharata:13:32.32	Those who always behave rightly toward mother, father and teachers, as you do, tiger of the Vrishnis: having said so, he ceased.
Therefore you too, Kaunteya, rightly honour ancestors, gods, the twice-born and guests, by which you will gain the desired goal.
[Bhishma said:] This is the most important duty, Bharata, of a consecrated king: the practice for brahmanas; one wishing the utmost happiness should always honour learned old brahmanas.
He should also honour townspeople, countryfolk and learned brahmanas with conciliation, gifts of enjoyment and salutations.
He should mark this as the king's most important duty always: as he protects himself and his sons, so he should protect them.
And those among them who are most worthy of honour he should honour firmly; when they are at peace, that whole kingdom shines.
They are to be honoured, to be saluted, to be protected like ancestors; the world's course depends on them as beings on Vasava.
By magic and means they might burn with their splendour; angry, fierce and truly valiant, they might leave nothing.
I do not see an end to them nor open directions; angry, they look about like tongues of fire in forest fires.
Their bold qualities are great, like wells covered with grass, pure, like another sky.
Brahmanas, O lord of men, are the greatly fortunate priests of ancestors, gods, men, serpents and rakshasas.
The twice-born cannot be conquered by gods, ancestors, gandharvas, rakshasas, asuras or pishachas.
They could make the non-divine divine and the divine non-divine; the one they favour becomes king, the one they hate is defeated.
Those fools who slander brahmanas, skilled in blame and praise, causing fame and infamy, high and low, king, make the twice-born constantly hate.
The man whom brahmanas praise prospers; he whom brahmanas revile is defeated in an instant.
The Shakas, Yavanas and Kambojas, those and those kshatriya peoples, have become shudras by not seeing brahmanas.
The Dravidas, Kalingas, Pulindas, Ushinaras, Kaulas, Sarpas and Mahishakas, those and those kshatriya peoples,
have become shudras by not seeing brahmanas. Defeat is better than victory over them, best of the victorious.
He who would kill all this, and he who kills a brahmana, are not equal; the great sages say the killing of a brahmana is a great fault.
Slander of the twice-born must never be heard; one should sit with face down, silent, or rise and go.
No one has been born or will be born on earth here who can live happily in opposition to brahmanas.
The wind is hard to hold in a fist, the moon hard to touch by hand, the earth hard to bear on the head; brahmanas are hard to conquer on earth.
With enjoyments, ornaments and whatever else they wish, they are always to be honoured, saluted and protected by kings like ancestors; thence comes peace for the kingdom, as for beings from Vasava.
Let there be born in the kingdom a pure brahmana of Brahmic splendour, and a great-chariot kshatriya, scorcher of enemies, is to be sought.
A brahmana of good birth, knower of dharma and of sharp vows, should be settled in one's house, king; there is nothing higher than that.
The gods accept the offering given to brahmanas; ancestors and all beings; there is nothing higher than them.
The sun, moon, wind, earth, water, sky and directions all, entering a brahmana, always eat food.
The ancestors do not eat of him whose brahmanas do not eat, and the gods too do not eat of the sinner, hater of brahmanas.
When brahmanas are pleased, the ancestors and likewise the gods are always pleased, king; there is no need to hesitate over this.
So too those whose offering it is are pleased; they do not perish after death but go to the highest goal.
With whatever offering a man would satisfy brahmanas, with that same the ancestors and gods are pleased.
From a brahmana is that being, from whom creatures arise, from whom he arises, and after death where he goes.
He knows the way to heaven and to hell, and both the coming and not coming; a brahmana, best of the two-footed, bull of the Bharatas, knows his dharma by wisdom.
Those who follow him do not meet defeat; they do not perish after death but go and do not meet defeat.
Those who take up the word that has come from a brahmana's mouth, practised and great-souled, do not meet defeat.
For kshatriyas who blaze with splendour and strength, splendours and strengths are appeased in brahmanas alone.
The Bhrigus conquered the Talajanghas, the Angirases the Nipas, Bharadvaja the Vitahavyas and the Ailas, bull of the Bharatas,
and they conquered the Chitrayudhas too, these with black antelope skins for banners; having thrown away the pots, one may begin as one who crosses over.
Whatever is said, heard or seen in the world is all hidden in brahmanas alone, like fire in wood.
On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, a conversation of Vasudeva and the Earth, bull of the Bharatas.
[Vasudeva said:] Mother of all beings, I ask you a doubt, auspicious one: by what deed does a householder wash away sin?
[The Earth said:] "He should serve brahmanas only; for this is the highest purifier; serving brahmanas, all stain perishes.
From this comes prosperity, from this fame, from this understanding is born, for others and others, and those beyond.
The man whom brahmanas praise prospers; he who is reviled by brahmanas is soon defeated.
As a lump of clay thrown into the great ocean perishes, so bad conduct leads to defeat.
See the mark placed on the moon and the salt water in the sea; and Mahendra is marked with a thousand marks.
By their very power that one became thousand-eyed, Shatakratu; see, Madhava, what kind.
Wishing prosperity, fame and worlds, Madhusudana, a man, pure and self-possessed, should abide by the approval of brahmanas."
Hearing this speech of the Earth, Madhusudana said "Well, well," and honoured the Earth.
Hearing this comparison, Partha, you should always honour the best of brahmanas, restrained; then you will gain the good.
[Bhishma said:] Brahmanas, dear one, are all our friends; honoured, with pleased faces, they bless us with auspicious words.
Brahmanas, dear one, with anger arisen, would strike all our enemies with harsh words if they were not honoured.
Here the verses sung by Brahma are recited by the knowers of old; the creator, having created the twice-born, placed them as before:

You have nothing else to do here higher by rule; guarded, guard Brahman; thereby your good is lovely.
mahabharata:13:35.6	Doing only your own work, Brahmic fortune will be yours; you will become the standard of all beings and gain leadership.
mahabharata:13:35.7	A wise brahmana should not do the work of a shudra, for doing a shudra's work obstructs dharma.
mahabharata:13:35.8	Shri, understanding, splendour and glorious power you will gain by study alone, spotless greatness.
mahabharata:13:35.9	Having offered at the Ahavaniya fire, established in great fortune, first eaters of the produce, arranged by Brahmic prosperity.
I think their strength is greater, as for a king with austerity; they are hard to approach, fierce, impetuous and quick in action.
Some of them have the nature of lions, others of tigers, others of boars and deer, others of elephants.
Some are soft as cotton, others touch like the makara; some strike by speech, others destroy the eye.
Some are like venomous snakes, some dull; various are the conducts of brahmanas here, Yudhishthira.
The Mekalas, Dramidas, Kashas, Paundras, Kollagiras, Shaundikas, Daradas, Darvas, Chauras, Shabaras and Barbaras,
the Kiratas and Yavanas, those and those kshatriya peoples, have become shudras by not seeing brahmanas.
By contempt of brahmanas, the asuras lie in the water; by the grace of brahmanas, the gods dwell in heaven.
The sky cannot be touched, the Himalaya cannot be moved, the Ganga cannot be stopped by a dam; brahmanas are hard to conquer on earth.
The earth cannot be ruled in opposition to brahmanas; brahmanas, great souls, are gods even of the gods.
Honour them constantly with gifts and service, if you wish to enjoy this earth girdled by the sea.
The splendour of brahmins is appeased by receiving gifts, sinless one; those who do not wish to accept gifts are also to be protected by you, sinless one.
Shakra, in an unrecognised form, becoming matted-haired and dusty-red, taking an ugly form, asked Shambara a question.
By what conduct, Shambara, do you stand above your own people, and by what do they consider you best? Tell me, who ask.
[Shambara said:] "I never envy brahmanas nor the grandfather Brahma; I honour brahmanas who speak scriptures as I please.
Having heard, I do not slight, nor ever offend; I ask those to be honoured, and I take the feet of the wise.
They speak confidently and always restrain me; among the heedless I am heedless-not, among the asleep I am awake.
They, the instructors, pour on me, engaged in the path of scripture, devoted to Brahman, without envy, as bees pour honey into honey.
Whatever they say, pleased, I take it with wisdom, always thinking of composure of the self, agreeable.
So I, a taster of the juices first created by speech, stand above my own people as the moon above the stars."
[Soma said:] "Brahmanas all succeed by austerity, their strength being speech; kings have strength of arm; the twice-born have the weapon of speech.
One should study even living abroad, living in many bad dwellings, free of anger and pride, an ascetic equal in sight.
Even one of good birth who studies all the Vedas in his father's house, boasting, they call a villager.
The earth swallows these two, like a serpent lying in a hole: a king who does not fight and a brahmana who does not travel.
Excess of pride destroys the prosperity of a man of little wisdom; a maiden is spoiled by pregnancy and a twice-born by staying at home.
Hearing this from Soma of wonderful sight, my father honoured brahmanas, and so did I, of great vows."
[Bhishma said:] Hearing this speech that fell from the mouth of the lord of danavas, Shakra honoured the twice-born and gained the lordship of Mahendra.
[Bhishma said:] Some have the excellent secret vow of action: whoever begs whatever, "I shall give everything."
We have heard that without troubling the group of servants; for one who troubles servants lowers himself.
A worthy vessel may be one who is unprecedented, or one who has long lived with one, or one who comes from afar: so the wise know.
[Yudhishthira said:] Without troubling servants and with non-violence to dharma, we should know the worthy vessel in truth, to whom a gift does not cause remorse.
[Bhishma said:] Officiants, priests, teachers, pupils, relatives and kinsmen are all to be honoured and respected when joined with learning and conduct.
Those who behave otherwise than this are all unworthy of honour; therefore one should always examine men attentively.
Freedom from anger, truthful speech, non-violence, self-control, honesty, freedom from malice, absence of excess of pride, modesty, patience, austerity and peace.
In whom these are seen, and not forbidden acts, Bharata, established by feeling, that vessel deserves honour.
A brahmana who thinks himself learned, a reviler of the Veda, devoted to the useless science of logic and reasoning,
speaking arguments among the good, a winner by causeless arguing, and always a reviler and over-talkative against brahmanas,
suspicious of all, foolish, childish, harsh-voiced: such a one, dear one, is to be understood; they call him a man-dog.
As a dog is let loose to bark and to kill, so for conversation and for the killing of all scripture are those of little learning, bad reasoners, seen and touched, bad pundits.
One should follow those who know Shruti, Smriti, Itihasa, Purana, the Aranyaka and the Veda, the learned who know much and who know the essence.
The course of the world and dharma and what is good for oneself should be considered; a man acting so prospers for everlasting years.
Having discharged the debt to the gods, to the sages, to the ancestors, to brahmins, and fifth to guests,
in turn, by pure and well-cleansed action, a householder doing deeds so does not fall from dharma.
[Bhishma said:] On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Narada and the wanton woman Panchachuda.
Long ago the wise divine sage Narada, roaming the worlds, saw the apsara Panchachuda, a woman of Brahma's world, blameless.
Seeing her lovely in every limb, the sage asked the apsara: "I have a doubt in my heart; tell me that, slender-waisted one."
Thus addressed, she replied to the brahmana Narada: "If it is within my domain, I shall tell you, if you think me able."
[Narada said:] "I shall not engage you in a matter outside your domain, fair one. I wish to hear from you the nature of women, fair-faced one."
[Bhishma said:] Hearing his words, the best of apsarases replied to the divine sage: "I, a woman, being good, cannot blame women."
You know which women are and of what kind by nature; you ought not to engage me, divine sage, in such a question.
The divine sage said to her, "Speak the truth, slender-waisted one; there is a fault in untruth; in truth there is no fault."
[Panchachuda said:] "Women of good family, beautiful, with protectors, do not stay within limits; that fault is in women, Narada.
There is nothing else more sinful than women; women are the root of faults, as you too know.
Having got an opening, women cannot wait for husbands well known, prosperous, suited and under their control.
This is the evil dharma of us women, lord: that casting off shame we resort to sinful men.
Women wish for the very man who asks for a woman, comes close and does a little service.
From men's not asking and from fear of relatives, the unrestrained women stay within limits with their husbands.
There is none unapproachable for them, and no fixity in age; ugly or handsome, they enjoy a male just as a male.
Women do not stay with their husbands from fear or from compassion or for wealth, nor from the bond of kin or family.
Women of good family long for women who are in youth, well adorned and clothed and who act as they please.
Even women who are always highly esteemed and guarded as dear cling to hunchbacks, the blind, the dull and the dwarfish.
Even to the lame, divine sage, and other despised men, there is none in this world unapproachable to women, great sage.
If men are not found somehow, they act upon one another; they do not stay with their husbands.
From not getting men, from fear of relatives and from fear of death and bondage, they become self-guarded.
Fickle by nature, hard to serve, hard to grasp by feeling: for a wise man here women are as speech is.
Fire is not satisfied with wood, nor the great ocean with rivers, nor the ender with all beings, nor fair-eyed women with men.
Here is another secret of all women, divine sage: on seeing a man to the heart's liking, a woman's womb moistens.
Women do not forgive the husband who is the giver of desires, the maker of mind's comfort and protector, the highest.
They do not value many desires and enjoyments or the heaping of ornaments as they value favour in love.
The ender, Death, the underworld, the mare's-mouth fire, a razor's edge, poison, a snake, fire: women are all that in one.
From where the five great elements, from where the worlds were ordained by the creator, from where men and women were made, there too, Narada, are the faults in women."
[Yudhishthira said:] Thus, tiger among men, how can these women be guarded by a man here? You ought to explain that to me.
These cheat men with illusions of their own making, and no man who comes into their hands is freed; like cows taking new grass, they take new men after new.
The illusion of Shambara, of Namuchi, of Bali and of Kumbhinasi: all those, know, are women.
They laugh with one laughing, weep with one weeping, and by pleasant words take the unwelcome in time.
In the scripture that Ushanas knows and what Brihaspati knows, the minds of women are not surpassed; how can they be guarded by men?
Untruth is truth they say, and truth also so, untruth; how can such women be guarded by men here, hero?
By drawing out the minds of women, I think, slayer of foes, the treatises on wealth were made by the good, Brihaspati and others.
[Bhishma said:] On this I shall tell you an ancient Itihasa, how protection was done long ago by the great-souled Vipula.
And how wanton women were created by Brahma, bull of the Bharatas, and for what purpose; that I shall tell you, dear one, lord of the earth.
There is nothing more sinful than women, son; a wanton woman is blazing fire, an illusion born of Maya, lord; a razor's edge, poison, a snake, death: women are all that in one.
These creatures, mighty-armed, are righteous, so we have heard; they go to godhood by themselves, and then fear came to the gods.
Then the gods came to the grandfather, scourge of foes, told him their mind and stood silent with faces down.
Knowing what was in the minds of those gods, the grandfather, the lord, for the bewilderment of men, created women as magical creatures.
In the first creation, Kaunteya, women here were virtuous; but those born from the magical creation of Prajapati were not.
To them the grandfather gave desires as desired; those wanton women, greedy for desire, then harassed men.
The lord of the gods created anger as the helper of desire; all creatures, attached, came under the power of desire and anger.
For women no rite, so dharma is set; they are without sense-organs and without mantras, and untruth, so Shruti says.
The Prajapati gave to women bed and seat, ornaments, food and drink, ignobleness, bad speech and sexual pleasure.
A man cannot in any way guard them; even the maker of the universe could not, dear one, how then men here?
By words, or by killing and binding, or by various hardships, women cannot be guarded, for they are always unrestrained.
But this, tiger among men, I heard earlier: how Vipula formerly guarded his teacher's wife.
There was a greatly fortunate sage famed as Devasharman, whose wife named Ruchi was incomparable in beauty on earth.
Gods, gandharvas and danavas were maddened by her beauty, and especially, king, the slayer of Vritra, Pakashasana.
The great sage Devasharman, knowing the ways of women, guarded his wife as well as he could and with all effort.
And he knew Purandara to go after others' wives; therefore he guarded his wife with effort.
Once, dear one, the sage, wishing to perform a sacrifice, thought: "How should my wife be guarded?"
Having considered in mind the arrangement of protection, that great ascetic called his dear pupil Vipula, a Bhargava, and said:

I shall go to perform a sacrifice. The lord of the gods always desires this Ruchi, my son; guard her as you can.
mahabharata:13:40.23	You must be unheedless of Purandara always; he takes many forms, lifter of Bhrigu's line.
Thus told by him, Vipula, the ascetic of controlled senses, always of fierce austerity, O king, with splendour like fire and sun,
knowing dharma and truthful, said "So be it"; and again, great king, he asked his famed teacher:
What forms does Shakra take when he comes, sage? What body and splendour does he have? You ought to tell me.
Then the blessed one told the great-souled Vipula truly of Shakra's magic, Bharata.

Slayer of Bala, Pakashasana, brahmana sage, has much magic; again and again he assumes those many forms.
mahabharata:13:40.29	He becomes crowned, thunderbolt-bearing, bow-bearing, wearing a diadem and bound earrings; in a moment he looks like a Chandala.
mahabharata:13:40.30	He becomes tufted, matted, bark-clad, son, and large-bodied, then stout, then lean again.
mahabharata:13:40.31	He changes colour to fair, dark and black; ugly and handsome, young and old.
mahabharata:13:40.32	Learned, dull, mute, short and tall, brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya, shudra, in reverse or direct order, Shatakratu becomes.
mahabharata:13:40.33	He takes the form of a parrot or crow, swan or cuckoo, and the form of lions, tigers and elephants.
mahabharata:13:40.34	He takes divine, demonic and kingly forms; very thin, with limbs broken by wind, a bird, deformed.
mahabharata:13:40.35	Four-footed and of many forms, a fool again, and he takes the form of flies, gnats and the like.
mahabharata:13:40.36	He cannot be grasped by Vipula or anyone, dear one, nor even by the maker of the universe by whom this world was made.
mahabharata:13:40.37	Vanishing, Shakra is again seen by the eye of knowledge; and becoming wind, the king of gods again appears.
mahabharata:13:40.38	Pakashasana constantly makes such forms; therefore guard this slender-waisted woman with great effort.
mahabharata:13:40.39	Let the lord of the gods, best of Bhrigus, not lick Ruchi as an evil dog licks an offering placed at its proper time.
Having so said, the sage Devasharman, greatly fortunate, then went to perform the sacrifice, best of Bharatas.
Hearing his teacher's word, Vipula became absorbed in thought, and made the highest protection against the mighty lord of the gods.

What can I do in guarding my teacher's wife? The lord of the gods is a magician, unassailable and mighty.
mahabharata:13:40.43	Pakashasana cannot be guarded against by closing the hermitage or the hut; his forms are many.
mahabharata:13:40.44	Shakra might assail the teacher's wife in the form of wind; therefore, entering her, I shall stay as Ruchi today.
mahabharata:13:40.45	Or this woman cannot be guarded by me by manly means, for the blessed lord of bay horses is heard to have many forms.
mahabharata:13:40.46	So by the power of yoga I shall guard her from Pakashasana; I shall enter her limbs with my limbs to guard her.
mahabharata:13:40.47	If my teacher, of divine knowledge and great austerity, were to see this wife Ruchi defiled, he would doubtless curse me in anger.
mahabharata:13:40.48	And she cannot be guarded by men as other women can; the lord of gods is a magician; ah, I have come into doubt.
mahabharata:13:40.49	The teacher's command must be done here; if I do this, it would be a wonder done by me.
mahabharata:13:40.50	Entering by yoga the body of the teacher's wife, I would have no offence, being released from the form of rajas.
mahabharata:13:40.51	As a traveller lodges on the road in an empty hall, so I shall lodge today in the teacher's wife's body.
mahabharata:13:40.52	As a drop of water unattached and trembling on a lotus leaf, so I shall dwell composed in her body.
Thus having considered dharma, the Vedas in every way, his great austerity and his teacher's own,
having resolved so in mind, that Bhargava made supreme effort at protection; hear how, king.
Sitting near the teacher's wife, the great ascetic Vipula tempted the blameless-limbed seated woman with conversation.
Joining the rays of his eyes to the rays of her eyes, Vipula entered her body like wind into the sky.
With mark to mark and face to face, motionless, the sage stayed within, like a shadow.
Then Vipula, holding fast the teacher's wife's body, dwelt engaged in guarding her, and she did not notice him.
And rejected by him, I do not wish to live today; I have been abandoned by my teacher and am defiled, Narada.
While Dhritarashtra, king of kings, was saying this to Yudhishthira, the sage Vyasa, son of Satyavati, came up and spoke.
Those who had been protected by the lord of the world, seeing the unprotected Partha as protector, wailed.
In the place of the Ashvins, shining with their own splendour, the descendant of the Kurus saw Nakula and Sahadeva.
